A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients. You can think of T3 Code as an open source "bring-your-own-subscription" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor. ## What makes T3 Code special? We have over 500,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on. ### 1. Open at the core T3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way. ### 2. Performance without compromise Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact. ### 3. Remote ready The architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported. ### 4. Multi-surface T3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**. **Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing "app.t3.codes" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable. **Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app. **Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely. ## A note from Theo I like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising. Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. 66	
67	The most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:
68	
69	- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
70	- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`
71	- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is "not supported here".
72	- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.
73	- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.
74	- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.
75	- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.

141	
142	For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is an install step, not a blocker. Run `vp run mobile:install <ios|android> [device-id]` on the device host before starting Metro; it targets the only booted simulator or connected Android device when the id is omitted. It installs the dev client for this checkout's native fingerprint from the shared cache in seconds and builds only when no machine has built it yet, so prefer it over `expo run:*`, `xcodebuild`, or `gradlew`, which rebuild from scratch. Its stdout is one JSON line; build output goes to the log it names. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.
143	
144	## Evals
145	
146	`evals/` checks how real models behave with T3 Code's model-facing text: agent instructions, MCP tool descriptions and schemas, and generated titles. Before you change that text, read [evals/README.md](evals/README.md) and run the evals it names. When you fix a model behavior bug, add a case that fails before the fix.
147	
148	## Pull requests
149	
150	- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
151	- If `origin` is git.cafe, follow [GitCafe mirror](docs/operations/development.md#gitcafe-mirror-optional): push to `origin`, open and track PRs with `cafe` and their git.cafe URLs, and keep `gh` for merging.
152	- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
153	- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
154	- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
155	- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
156	- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.
157	- When babysitting: call `watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you on checks, comments, or conflicts. Do not poll or sleep. Verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.
158	
159	## Documentation
160	
161	Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.
162	
163	- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
164	- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
165	- A local reason the code can't show goes in a short nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
166	- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
167	- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
168	- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
169	- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.
170	
171	## Plans and work artifacts
172	
173	- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
174	- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
175	- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.
176	
177	## How it works
178	
179	Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.
180	
181	Architecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`
182	
183	## Where code lives
184	
185	- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
186	- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
187	- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
188	- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
189	- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
190	- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency. If it is missing (sparse checkout), read a file with `git show origin/main:.repos/<path>`.
191	
192	## Taste
193	
194	- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
195	- Client mutations use `createEnvironmentRpcCommand`. Add protected methods to `CLIENT_GUARDED_RPC_SCOPES` in contracts and use the command's `permissionAtom` for UI availability. Grants are checked at execution against the destination environment; the server remains authoritative. Keep raw RPC clients inside `rpc/`, and extend the permission behavior tests when adding a protected method.
196	- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
197	- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations. See [Web UI](docs/internals/web-ui.md).
198	- Reusable Effect functions use `Effect.fn("Service.operation")` with a stable span name, not a
199	  function wrapping `Effect.gen`. Keep `Effect.gen` for inline programs and layer construction.
200	  Use `Effect.fnUntraced` only when spans would be too frequent (stream chunks, per-event
201	  projection, tight loops) or duplicate an existing tracing boundary; explain that choice nearby.
202	  Named `Effect.fn` creates a span; the unnamed form does not. Preserve existing span names and
203	  options, and pass combinators as additional function-builder arguments.
204	- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
205	- Default to no comment. Write one only for a constraint, an external quirk, or an invariant the code can't show, in one line where you can and four at most. Don't restate names or signatures, narrate steps, record history, or explain the fix you just made; the PR carries that. `t3code/no-low-value-comments` enforces the length cap and the mechanical cases.
206	- React effects are for synchronizing with something outside React. Derive in render and act in handlers instead of syncing state, but don't hide real lifecycle work in refs or stores to dodge one. The `t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync` lint rule reports every effect; one that stays states its reason with `// oxlint-disable-next-line t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync -- <why>`.
207	- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
208	- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.
209	
210	## Additional tips
211	
212	- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
213	- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

name: Agent Context Budget

# Fails when a PR raises a value in agentContextBudget.json above main's. AgentContextBudget.test.ts
# keeps that file equal to the measured context, so the context cannot grow by editing the file.
# To accept growth on purpose, a maintainer adds the agent-context-increase label.
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled, unlabeled]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: agent-context-budget-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  budget:
    name: Agent context budget
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 5
    env:
      BUDGET: apps/server/src/provider/agentContextBudget.json
      ALLOW_INCREASE: ${{ contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'agent-context-increase') }}
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          sparse-checkout: apps/server/src/provider/agentContextBudget.json
          sparse-checkout-cone-mode: false

      - name: Compare with main
        run: |
          git fetch --quiet --depth=1 origin main
          if ! git cat-file -e "FETCH_HEAD:$BUDGET" 2>/dev/null; then
            echo "main has no agent context budget yet."
            exit 0
          fi
          git show "FETCH_HEAD:$BUDGET" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/main.json"
          grown=$(jq -r --slurpfile main "$RUNNER_TEMP/main.json" '
            to_entries[]
            | select($main[0][.key] != null and .value > $main[0][.key])
            | "\(.key): \($main[0][.key]) -> \(.value) (+\(.value - $main[0][.key]))"
          ' "$BUDGET")
          if [ -z "$grown" ]; then
            echo "Agent context is not larger than main."
            exit 0
          fi
          printf 'Agent context grew compared to main:\n%s\n' "$grown"
          if [ "$ALLOW_INCREASE" = "true" ]; then
            echo "Accepted by the agent-context-increase label."
            exit 0
          fi
          echo "::error file=$BUDGET::Agent context grew compared to main. Cut the added text, or ask a maintainer to add the agent-context-increase label."
          exit 1

# Testing

Rules for writing tests, and for asking for them in review. AGENTS.md carries the same writing rules under Verifying; change both together.

## What to test

- Test behavior that can break, such as orchestration and event-sourcing, provider protocol translation, auth and permission guards, persistence and migrations, external-format parsing, race fixes, and the logic a bug fix changed. Leave out tests for what types already guarantee, trivial logic, copy text, smoke runs, mock-call mirrors, callback wiring, and props rendered to static markup.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits.
- Test at one layer: the lowest one that fails on `main`. Do not repeat the case in a wrapper test, at each call site, or in web and mobile copies of the same logic.
- In review, ask for a missing test only when it would catch a real regression. Do not ask for one assertion per constant, label, or `switch` case. Flag a new test that breaks the rules above, and name the fix: fold it into the existing case or table, delete it, or keep one layer.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason, in an existing case of the module's test file where one fits), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures as their proof and no test: do not add UI tests for nitpicks, and do not ask for one in review when a capture already shows it. A server-only fix with no visible surface ships the test plus a short runtime transcript.

## Waiting for work

- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong. Concretely:
  - `it.effect` runs on a `TestClock`; `Effect.sleep` only advances through `TestClock.adjust`. `it.live` is wall-clock and only for subprocess or network fixtures.
  - No `yieldNow` or `sleep` polling loops. Await the `Deferred`, take from the `Queue`, or drain the worker.
  - No per-test timeout argument or `retry`. The project timeout is the ceiling, and flaky tests are fixed, not retried.
  - No `performance.now()` or `Date.now()` deltas. Assert on events and counts, not elapsed time.
  - Browser tests assert through `expect.element` or `vi.waitFor`, never `requestAnimationFrame` or `transitionend`.
  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.

## Web browser tests

# Performance regression checks

The v2 transport has a focused regression command:

```bash
vp run test:perf:v2-wire
```

It exercises the real v2 projection and client reducers. This matters because the older
built-app benchmark fixtures seed v1 orchestration events; running those fixtures against a v2
client can produce reassuring timings while missing the active transport path.

The v2 checks pin these invariants:

- Cold opens and history pages stop at about 1 MiB of encoded rows. A window that holds a user
  turn also stops at 10 user turns (20 on older pages) or 500 rows, so ordinary turns stay whole.
  Any other window, including the inside of one turn longer than 500 rows, stops at 75 rows. The
  snapshot query applies the same rule before it decodes payloads. Clients can opt into deferring
  large work groups until expansion. Messages and items outside those groups remain in normal
  history paging. Required control records and
  the at-least-one-row rule can exceed the byte target; it is not a hard cap.
- The bounded snapshot does not retain the full duplicate conversation-message table.
- Older activity is fetched in bounded HTTP pages and merged without disturbing the live scroll
  window.
- Clients with confirmed history paging opt into socket snapshot fallbacks that use the same
  bounded recent-history window and carry the cursor needed to fetch older history. Older clients
  and WebSocket-only starts retain the compatible full-snapshot fallback.
- Snapshot queries bound timeline reads per fork ancestor, not total rows: dependency and
  control records still accompany the window. Smaller socket frames alone do not establish a
  whole-server memory reduction.
- Resume catch-up checks the original 1 MiB persisted-payload budget before decoding, then
  replays at most 128 thread events and 1 MiB of projected event JSON before falling back to a
  snapshot. Raw JSON bytes are not a heap-memory cap. Raising this budget merely because output
  projects small can increase server allocations on repeated large tool updates.
- Raw command output, dynamic-tool result bodies, and inline file-change bodies are omitted at
  the wire boundary, including small outputs. Explicit failure flags and bounded result IDs
  preserve status and grouped action counts without shipping those bodies. Reasoning text,
  command lines, and search results ship when their work group loads. Subagent prompts and results
  and checkpoint control records still accompany the initial window.
  Persisted events remain complete; the existing diff endpoints still provide file content when
  requested.
  Explicit cross-environment transcript exports preserve full tool bodies so the destination
  agent can read the context. The export rejects timeline JSON above the file attachment limit
  before sending it; the client still applies its attachment limit to the complete file.
- Live command output reaches a client only through `orchestration.subscribeCommandOutput`, which
  an expanded command row opens and closes with itself. Raw output deltas are never orchestration
  events: adapters send them to the
  [command output hub](../../apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/CommandOutputHub.ts) ahead of
  ingestion, which keeps one bounded tail per running command and throttles each subscriber. Do not
  route output deltas through `turn_item.updated`: a busy command would flood the event store and
  block ingestion for every other thread.
- The initial shell contains active navigation rows only. Archived rows use the dedicated archive
  query, and transcript message bodies stay in thread detail regardless of message size.
- Shell resume sends deltas plus compact repository-enrichment metadata, not another full project
  and thread snapshot.
- Auto, steer, and restart sends resolve delivery from authoritative state inside the
  server's per-thread dispatch lock. Model selection and identified-checkpoint rollback also
  dispatch without first fetching a full thread projection when the server advertises support.
  Older servers retain projection-based validation. Explicit start sends already skipped that
  read, so this saving does not apply to every client send path.

When changing projection schemas, paging, shell synchronization, or thread state, run this command
alongside the focused package typechecks and a real-client pass on every affected surface. The
transport performance fixtures validate contract encoding and compare pre-compression RPC JSON
for the same synthetic workload, preserving historical application-object counts separately.
These are neither compressed WebSocket captures nor measurements of server RSS, and command
fixtures exclude unrelated settings calls and subscription events. Payload budgets belong in
these tests so regressions fail locally. The transfer budget integration test
(`apps/server/integration/transferBudgetV2.integration.test.ts`) sends the opt-ins current clients
send and caps the decoded bytes and rows of the bounded snapshot and one older page for a 900-row
agent turn, and of the cold-connect shell for a sidebar of settled threads and idle subagents. When
clients gain an opt-in, add it to the test's client queries and give a fixture the data it saves.

## Event store and startup

Sequence cursors must seek an index rather than scan retained history. The application sequence
index contains project events and v2 thread events; the per-thread sequence index contains only v2
thread events. Legacy-only and unknown threads must return zero without scanning other threads.
Catch-up queries keep sequence ranges and optional thread or command predicates indexable.

Startup selects recovery candidates from current projection state before reading full thread
projections. Candidate selection includes queued runs, pending runtime requests, live provider
sessions, background work, and unfinished delegated deliveries. Archived threads still participate
where recovery requires them. Completed thread history is not loaded merely to discover that no
work remains.

Projection verification decodes canonical rows in bounded pages, including shared provider records
and fork ancestry. Rebuild replays event pages through a fixed sequence within its transaction;
it must not collect the entire event log before projecting it.

The focused regression coverage lives in `OrchestrationEventStore.sequence.test.ts`,
`ProjectionRecovery.test.ts`, and the provider runtime recovery tests under `apps/server/src`.

## Background work and navigation

The settlement worker reads active, unpinned threads without explicit settlement overrides from
`ProjectionStore.getSettlementCandidates`. It reads the latest run and user-message timestamps,
rejects active runs and pending requests, and checks background work using the same derivation as
the shell. It does not load archived histories, fork ancestry, transcript counts, or provider
sessions. The orchestrator still validates the current thread before applying settlement.

Read receipts use `ProjectionStore.getThread` to load only canonical thread metadata. A visit
advances `lastVisitedAt` monotonically without changing `updatedAt` or decoding history. Shell
queries use a covering thread/run index for item counts and a partial index for nonterminal
background items, including idle items. Latest user-message reads use an index ordered by update
time.

Command palette results keep live VCS and linked pull-request queries leased to the visible
viewport, including a small overscan region. Cached badges remain available while leases are
released. Local Git status reads skip divergence calculations; callers that need ahead/behind
counts keep the full status path. Cached fetch failures share the existing backoff and log only
the actual failed attempt. Unchanged desktop environment bootstrap reads retain their array
identity so polling does not invalidate subscribers.

Local trace records and provider event logs use asynchronous, serialized file writes and rotation.
Batching synchronous appends still stalls the server event loop on slow storage, especially on
Windows. While a trace write is slow, producers keep up to one trace file of records, so the spans
that time a stall survive it; records drop only while the disk stays stuck. Provider logging
retains backpressure. Shutdown drains accepted writes before closing their scope.

Our setup already matches t3code's on most points. We've adopted its `AGENTS.md` structure, oxlint and oxfmt, the comment and suppression-reason rules, knip, and tsc-rs. We also have a few things it lacks, like `check:refs` and the contracts package for IPC. So the gap is small. I made no changes. I read t3code in a scratch clone outside the worktree, and the one lint run on our `src` was read-only.

## Worth doing, in order

1. **`AGENTS.md` has a stale code map.** It says the library grid, cards and Spaces UI live in `src/App.tsx`. They live in `src/features/library`, `src/features/spaces` and `src/features/shell`. `App.tsx` is a 779-line wiring file. The map also omits `packages/contracts` (the IPC command list), `packages/ingestion-shared`, `extension/` (an entry point) and `scripts/`. Agents follow this map, so it's the cheapest fix with the biggest effect.

2. **Add `bun run check:changed`.** t3code has one script that runs lint, format, knip, typecheck and the sibling tests for just the changed files. Our `AGENTS.md` asks agents to assemble that by hand, and `bun run check` is too heavy for that. A trimmed version of about 60 lines would do: `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on changed files, plus `bun test` for `foo.test.ts` next to a changed `foo.ts`.

3. **Run tests on Windows in CI.** The `frontend` job runs `bun test` on `ubuntu-24.04`. The Windows jobs only build the installer. Asset containment (`isInside` in `electron/storage/shared.ts`) depends on `node:path` separators. The traversal test therefore only proves POSIX behavior, while the app ships on Windows. t3code has a Windows test lane, though only on manual dispatch. I'd run `bun test electron/` on `windows-latest`. I haven't confirmed the suite passes there in CI, though it's developed on Windows.

4. **Tell agents where Effect's docs are.** `electron/` is built on Effect 4.0.6, and `AGENTS.md` never mentions it. That version ships its own `AGENTS.md` and `ai-docs/` in `node_modules/effect`, so t3code's vendored `.repos/effect-smol` isn't needed. One pointer line is enough. Effect's guidance prefers `Effect.fn("name")` for reusable functions, and our `electron/` has no `Effect.fn(` calls. Treat that as optional.

5. **Turn on the React rules we've disabled.** t3code runs `set-state-in-effect`, `refs`, `immutability` and `exhaustive-effect-dependencies` as errors. We have them off. Enabling them gives 25 diagnostics in 14 files: 13 `set-state-in-effect`, 8 `refs`, 2 `immutability` and 2 `exhaustive-effect-dependencies`. These are mostly cascading-render patterns, which fits the performance principle. `react/purity` has zero hits and isn't in our config, so it can go on today.

6. **Lint the test rules that `AGENTS.md` only states in prose.** t3code enforces no sleeps, no wall-clock deltas, no per-test timeouts and no skips without a reason. We have zero violations today, so this guards against drift rather than fixing anything. Port two or three of the rules only if agents start regressing.

## Skip

- **Tooling and release machinery:** the `vite-plus` and pnpm toolchain, the provider package split, PR-size labels, and the vouch and triage bots.
- **`agent-context-budget` workflow:** it budgets the prompt text t3code injects into agents, not `AGENTS.md`.
- **`evals/`:** we have no model-facing text.
- **`docs/internals/` tree:** our `docs/README.md` defers it on purpose.
- **React Compiler with `no-manual-memo`:** we have 55 manual memo sites. t3code's docs say bailouts are silent and need a coverage test to catch them, so at most a spike.

- Data flows one way. Into your sandbox, never back out. Copy in, never symlink. Never write your test edits back to the source.
- Bring assets only for the items your flow needs. Do not copy the whole asset store to test one card.
- The committed demo seed in `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the safe default for UI work. It shuffles with a fixed seed so the order is mixed but stable. Prefer it over real data when it covers your case.
- Never commit a copied database, a real user item, or a downloaded model. The gitignore already excludes run artifacts. Keep it that way.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works: `bun test <files>` for the tests you touched, `bunx oxlint <files>` and `bunx oxfmt --check <files>` for what you changed, and `bun run typecheck` (fast enough to run whole). The full check is `bun run check`, which mirrors the CI frontend job. Do not run it unless you changed something broad or the user asked.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No full `bun test` sweep or full `tsc` unless asked. CI owns the full suite.
- A test earns its place by guarding something that breaks quietly: extraction and sanitizing, embed allowlists, OCR scoring, queue leases and recovery, migrations and persistence, asset path containment and range requests, deep link and external-format parsing, ordering and race guarantees, and `liquidGlassShape`. A test added with a bug fix stays; mark it `// regression: #NNN` if its name doesn't say so.
- Don't write tests the types already prove, trivial logic, basic DOM behavior, static-markup renders, mock-call mirrors, smoke tests, duplicate table rows, or wall-clock and perf asserts.
- Ingestion and background changes ship with focused tests for that behavior. A behavior change with no test is unfinished.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures and no test.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits. Test at the lowest layer that fails on `main`, not again in a wrapper or at each call site.
- Background work is async. Await the real signal: a job drain, a lease state, an event. No fixed sleeps, per-test timeouts, retries, `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` deltas, polling loops, or skips without a reason.
- UI changes need one real pass in the running app before you call them done (the `verify-inkling` skill drives it). Preview for layout, full app for anything native. Take a screenshot through the harness so the user can see it. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Clean up what you launched when you are done.
- There are no local hooks. CI runs the frontend checks and Electron package smoke tests.

## Pull requests
## How it works

Capture creates the item immediately, then background jobs do the slow parts. Normalize, extract text and metadata, run OCR or PDF extraction or article parsing, generate embeddings. Writes to items update the FTS index through triggers. The user keeps browsing or does something else while jobs run. A job can be retried, its lease can expire, and interrupted jobs recover on restart.

Search combines exact FTS over content, notes, and OCR text with semantic similarity over local embeddings. Smart Spaces are saved searches whose query runs each time their items load, so they need no background job.

The Electron main process owns files, the job queue, the database, and model execution. The renderer gets a narrow preload bridge, not raw filesystem or shell access. Fetched HTML is untrusted. It gets sanitized, embeds pass an allowlist, scripts and event handlers are stripped.

Full reasoning in `docs/tech-stack.md`. Behavior contract in `docs/product-behavior.md`.

## Where code lives

- `src/` is the React and TypeScript frontend. Entry at `src/main.tsx`.
- `src/lib/ingestion/` is the capture and extraction pipeline. Defuddle, metadata fallback, sanitizing, video link handling.
- `src/components/` holds shared pieces such as the card media (`ItemMedia.tsx`), the expanded item overlay, and the PDF viewer. The library grid, cards, and Spaces UI live in `src/App.tsx`, and the reader is `src/ReaderView.tsx`.
- `electron/` holds the desktop main process, preload bridge, SQLite storage, job queue, PDF/OCR, embeddings, and packaging inputs.
- `benchmarks/` holds the corpus, the harness, expected outputs, and results. Of the results, only `results-latest.json` and `summary.md` are tracked.
- `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the committed demo library for UI work.

## Goal
Add `bun run check:changed`: one command an agent or dev runs while iterating and before pushing. It runs the fast subset of CI's checks for only what the branch changed. `bun run check` (the full CI mirror) stays as is. Inspiration is t3code's `scripts/check-changed.ts` (https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/scripts/check-changed.ts), but ours must be much smaller: yagni, aim for roughly 100 lines. ## Behavior
- `bun run check:changed` compares against `git merge-base HEAD origin/main`; optional first argument is another ref. If there is no merge base, print a one-line hint to `git fetch origin` and exit 1.
- Changed files = `git diff --name-only --no-renames <base>` plus untracked files (`git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`). Only files that still exist are passed to tools. No changes -> print so and exit 0.
- Steps (run concurrently, print each step's output when it finishes, then a pass/fail summary, exit non-zero if any failed):
  1. `oxlint` on changed JS/TS files (`bunx oxlint <files>` or the local binary; match how package.json's `lint` script invokes it).

  3. `bun test` on changed test files plus sibling tests of changed source files (`foo.ts` -> `foo.test.ts` in the same directory; also `.test.tsx`). Skip the step when none.
  4. `bun run knip` when any code file or package.json/knip.json changed.
  5. `bun run typecheck` when any code or tsconfig/package.json changed (it is fast enough to run whole).
- Must work on Windows (backslash paths from git are forward-slash; normalize anyway) and in a git worktree.
